client: I’m really nervous about meeting my partner’s friends this weekend. I keep worrying they won’t like me or think I’m not good enough for them. Honestly, I’m not sure if therapy can really help with this—it feels like my anxiety is just too big to overcome.
therapist: It sounds like you're feeling quite overwhelmed by these worries about meeting your partner's friends, and I hear a sense of doubt creeping in about whether things can improve. Let’s take a moment to unpack those thoughts—what specifically feels "too big" about this anxiety right now?
vocal_descriptors: very high pitch, soft-spoken, very rapid speech

client: It’s not just meeting his friends—it’s the fear that they’ll judge me or think I’m not good enough for him. I keep imagining them whispering about me after I leave, like I’m some kind of disappointment. It feels like I’m walking into a test I’m doomed to fail, and I don’t know how to stop thinking that way.
therapist: It seems like these thoughts are spiraling into a vivid, almost cinematic scenario of judgment and failure, which must feel really heavy to carry. What do you think it would mean if someone did judge you—what’s the worst-case scenario that’s playing out in your mind?
vocal_descriptors: very high pitch, moderate volume, very rapid speech

client: If someone judged me, it feels like they’d see me as completely incompetent or worthless. The worst-case scenario in my mind is that they’d tell everyone else, and I’d be completely isolated—no one would want to be around me anymore. It’s hard to shake that fear because it feels so real, even though I know it might not be logical.
therapist: I notice that while you’re describing these fears, your voice sounds even more intense than the words themselves—like this worry is really gripping you tightly. What do you think it might mean if, deep down, you believed that you’re not incompetent or worthless, even if someone judged you? Could that shift how you approach this situation?
vocal_descriptors: very high pitch, soft-spoken, very rapid speech

client:
I don't know... it's hard to imagine not believing I'm incompetent when I keep messing up at work. Even if I tried to believe otherwise, one mistake from me and it all comes crashing down. My boss's disappointed look just confirms what I already know about myself. 

When you ask if believing differently would help, it kind of makes me anxious - like now I'm failing at believing in myself too. What if I can't make that shift no matter how hard I try?
therapist: It sounds like you're carrying a heavy weight of self-doubt, where even the idea of changing these beliefs feels like another opportunity to "fail." That must be exhausting. Let’s slow down—what if we looked at this not as failing to believe in yourself, but as noticing how deeply these patterns of thinking have taken root? What does "messing up at work" actually look like in reality, versus how it feels in the moment?
vocal_descriptors: very high pitch, soft-spoken, fast speech

client: It feels like every time I make even a small mistake at work, I immediately spiral into thinking I’m incompetent and that everyone notices. Logically, I know people make mistakes all the time, but in the moment, it feels like the end of the world. I just can’t shake the fear that I’ll be exposed as a fraud or that I’m not cut out for this job.
therapist: I hear how these moments of making mistakes trigger such intense feelings of being exposed or not belonging—it’s like the weight of everything collapses onto that one moment. When you say it feels like the end of the world in those instances, can you recall a time when a mistake didn’t actually lead to the catastrophic outcome you feared? What happened instead?
vocal_descriptors: very high pitch, moderate volume, moderate-paced speech

client: Hmm, I guess there was a time last week when I messed up a small detail in a work presentation. I panicked and thought everyone would see me as incompetent, but no one even mentioned it. They just moved on. Even though nothing bad happened, I still felt that crushing shame afterward, like I’d failed somehow. It’s hard to shake that feeling, even when logically I know it wasn’t a big deal.
therapist: It’s interesting that even when the outcome was neutral—or even positive—the shame still lingered so strongly afterward. That tells me the real struggle isn’t just about the mistake itself, but how you interpret it afterward. What do you think keeps that cycle of shame going, even when the evidence doesn’t support it?
vocal_descriptors: very high pitch, moderate volume, fast speech

client:
I think part of me just expects to mess up, so even when things turn out okay, I still feel like I barely dodged disaster. It's like my brain keeps replaying the "what if" scenarios of everything going wrong, and that feeling sticks with me longer than the actual outcome. 

I know logically that the shame doesn't match what happened, but it's hard to shake this automatic reaction that I'm always one step away from failing.
therapist: It sounds like your mind is almost preparing for disaster, even when things turn out fine—like it’s stuck in a loop of anticipating failure. What do you think it would take to start shifting that expectation, even just a little, so that the "what if" scenarios don’t hold so much power over you?
vocal_descriptors: very high pitch, moderate volume, moderate-paced speech

client: I feel like my mind always jumps to the worst-case scenario because it’s trying to protect me from disappointment. But you’re right, it’s exhausting and makes everything feel harder than it needs to be. I just don’t know how to trust that things will be okay when so much feels uncertain. It’s like my brain won’t let me relax because it’s convinced something bad will happen if I do.
therapist: It sounds like your mind is working overtime to shield you from disappointment, but in doing so, it’s creating a lot of tension and exhaustion. What do you think it would feel like to allow yourself even a small moment of relaxation, where you’re not anticipating the worst? Could we explore what that might look like for you?
vocal_descriptors: very high pitch, soft-spoken, fast speech

client: Honestly, the idea of relaxing makes me more anxious. If I let my guard down even for a moment, I feel like something bad will happen—like I'll miss an important detail or someone will be upset with me. It's like my brain won't let me rest because it thinks constant worrying is the only way to stay safe.
therapist: It sounds like relaxing feels almost unsafe to you, as if worrying is the only way to stay prepared and avoid potential problems. That must be incredibly draining. What do you think it would take for your brain to start trusting that you can handle things, even if you’re not constantly on alert?
vocal_descriptors: very high pitch, soft-spoken, fast speech

client: That makes sense, but I don't know how to just stop worrying. What if something bad happens and I'm not prepared? My brain keeps telling me that relaxing means I'll miss important warning signs. It's like my anxiety is the only thing keeping me safe, even though I know it's exhausting.
therapist: It sounds like your anxiety feels like a necessary shield, even though it’s wearing you down. What if we tried to reframe this a bit—what would it look like to balance preparation with moments of rest, so you’re not carrying the full weight of worry all the time?
vocal_descriptors: very high pitch, soft-spoken, moderate-paced speech
